syllabus.clause: locating the pivot of a rotated array

at.step: In [4,5,6,7,0,1,2], searching for 0: is the left half [4,5,6,7] or the right half [0,1,2] guaranteed sorted, and which one does the search recurse into?

At every midpoint, comparing the range's first element to the middle element tells you which of the two halves is itself sorted ascending; once known, checking whether the target falls within that sorted half's own range is a single comparison, and the search recurses into whichever half can actually contain it.

Finding the rotation point itself — the index where the array's minimum sits — is the identical halving, aimed at a different predicate: search for the one boundary where a[mid] stops being greater than a[hi]. Same loop, same invariant, a one-line change in what gets compared.

When a[lo], a[mid] and a[hi] are all equal, that comparison tells you nothing about which half is sorted — both could be, or neither could look it. The only safe move is to shrink the range by one element at a time, and an array built from mostly one repeated value forces exactly that, almost every step, on the way to the single different value.

syllabus.clause: staircase search over a row- and column-sorted matrix

at.step: A matrix sorted ascending along every row and every column, but not sorted as one single flattened sequence — does ordinary binary search apply to it directly?

Starting from the top-right corner: if the target is smaller than the current cell, every cell below it is also too big, so the whole column can be dropped by stepping left; if the target is larger, every cell to its left is too small, so the whole row can be dropped by stepping down. Each comparison eliminates an entire row or an entire column.

A stronger matrix, where every row's last value is smaller than the next row's first value, is one ascending sequence read left to right, top to bottom — the whole matrix flattened. A midpoint index maps back to a cell by one division and one remainder, and ordinary binary search runs over it directly, in O(log(mn)). The staircase matrix from before has no such order: its second row starts lower than its first row ends.

syllabus.clause: the interview variants and their invariants

at.step: Three structures, three invariants to tell apart under pressure: which half is sorted, in a rotated array; which direction a corner walk shrinks, in a staircase matrix; whether a single flattened order even exists at all, between the two. Every search this chapter has built has assumed order already exists somewhere to exploit. The next question has none: finding the k-th smallest element with no sorted order to search at all. Quickselect and median-of-medians, next.
